spans.t: This is a book of thirteen days, made to go with the Camino Primitivo. It takes the
Confessions
of Augustine of Hippo one book at a time, thirteen books in thirteen days, in the order they stand. You read one day at a time, whether you are on the road or at home.
Every day has a morning reading of about five minutes and an evening reading of about three.
In the morning
there are three parts.

items.t: The passage.
A stretch of the
Confessions
, in the exact words of E. B. Pusey's old English translation,
Thou
and
Thee
and all. Read it twice, once aloud if you can. The English is archaic, and that slows the eye, which is half its use.
The reflection.

This part is ours, not Augustine's. It begins on the road, with a bench, a hill or a long afternoon, and lets the passage open it. It says what the passage says, where it is hard, and what it might change in an ordinary day. It is allowed to doubt.
For the walk.
A question to carry for the next hour, and one small practice that needs only attention.

spans.t: In the evening
there are two more.

items.t: At the end of the day.
A look back over the day you have lived, with two or three questions to lie down with.
A short prayer.
Original and brief. If you pray, pray it. If you pray differently, change the words. If you do not pray, say it as a wish.

spans.t: Why this book for this road

The CaminoPlus catalogue lists the Camino Primitivo as running from Oviedo to Santiago de Compostela, about 320 km, and rates it 4 on a scale of 1 to 5. It climbs through the mountains of Asturias before it crosses into Galicia, and it is a road of about two weeks. This book does not give stages. Thirteen days is the length of the reading, not a plan for the walk.
The pairing is an inward climb. The
Confessions
begins low down, with a baby and a stolen pear, and rises through grief, doubt and a garden to memory, time and rest. Augustine uses the picture himself. In the tenth book he speaks of
rising by degrees
, and in the last he writes
We ascend Thy ways that be in our heart, and sing a song of degrees

, a phrase that echoes the psalms called the songs of ascents, which are traditionally linked with pilgrims going up to Jerusalem. Both the road and the book are long, with hard stretches, and both are better taken in short pieces.
A Christian book, and who it is for
The
Confessions
is a Christian book, and it is a prayer. Augustine writes to God from the first line to the last, as a believer and as a bishop in the late Roman world, and that is why the whole thing says
Thou

. We say so plainly so that nobody is surprised. People walk the Camino for many reasons, faith, sport, grief, curiosity, a rest from work, and all of them are welcome here. You do not need to believe what Augustine believed to recognise a restless heart. Where he is hard to follow, the reflection says so.
The shape of the thirteen days
The days follow the books in order, and have a shape of their own.

items.t: Days 1 to 4: a young man and his restlessness.
A child, a stolen pear, a mother's tears and a lost friend.
Days 5 to 8: the search and the turn.
A teacher who disappointed, a bishop who read in silence, a glimpse that would not stay, and a garden.
Days 9 to 13: the climb inward.
A window at Ostia, memory, time, many ways of reading, and rest.

spans.t: Days 10 to 12 are the hardest. They are more philosophy than story, and the reflections say plainly where a passage is difficult. If a day will not open, read the passage aloud, say the prayer, and leave the rest for the morning.
On the road and at home

Read the morning part on a bench, in a bunk, or in a café while the soup arrives, then put the phone away and take the question with you. Read the evening part last of all, when the boots are off. At home, the morning goes with tea and the evening with bed. If your road is longer than thirteen days, read a day twice. If it is shorter, read a morning on one day and its evening on the next.
Two words you will meet.
Albergue
is the simple hostel where pilgrims sleep, often in bunks, often with a shared kitchen.
Buen Camino
is what walkers say to one another on the road, roughly, may your Way go well.

chapters.title: About the book and its author

spans.t: The man
Augustine of Hippo lived, by the usual reckoning, from about 354 to 430. The file we use gives no dates for his life, so those are the dates that reference books give, and we mark them
about
. What the
Confessions
itself tells us is where he moved. His father, it says, was
a poor freeman of Thagaste

, a small town in North Africa. Augustine studied and then taught rhetoric, the art of public speaking, at Thagaste and at Carthage, and later at Rome and Milan. In Milan he was baptised. The title page of the file calls him Saint Augustine, as the Church does, and Bishop of Hippo, the post he held when he wrote.
The book
The
Confessions

has thirteen books. The first nine tell his life, from infancy to the death of his mother at Ostia, the harbour town of Rome. The tenth turns from the past to the present and looks at memory. The eleventh is about time, and the last two are about the first chapter of Genesis. He wrote it about the year 400. The file dates it AD 401, and reference books generally give about 397 to 400, so we say about 400.
Confession
here means two things at once, owning a wrong and giving praise, and Augustine means both. The book is a prayer, and it is spoken to God, not to us. In the second book he asks,
To whom tell I this? not to Thee, my God; but before Thee to mine own kind
, and in the fourth he says that he would
still confess to Thee mine own shame in Thy praise
. We overhear, as it were, and are invited to say the words along with him.
Why it suits a pilgrim

Augustine is nearly always on the move in this book. The places it names, Thagaste, Madaura, Carthage, Rome, Milan and Ostia, are a chain of departures and arrivals, and a few of those journeys are at night, or by sea, or against someone's wishes. Yet its best-known sentence says that the heart is restless
until it repose in Thee

, and that sentence is not about a place. The book keeps both things in view: a restless traveller, and the thing he is travelling towards. That makes it an honest companion for a long walk, where the body goes one way and the mind goes several. It is also honest about being unfinished. It ends with a request, not with a conclusion.
What is hard, and what we left out

Augustine writes about the body, desire and sin as a Christian bishop looking back on his youth. He is much harder on his younger self than most readers would be, and he writes with real heat against the Manichees, a religious movement of his day which he had followed for about nine years. In the first book he says that in God's sight not even a day-old infant is pure from sin. These are his terms and his century, and we do not argue with him in the reader's ear. We chose passages that a walker can follow. Where one of them touches these matters, the reflection says so calmly (see Days 2, 3 and 8), and it does not make him say more or less than he says.

The last four books are more philosophy than story. They are about memory, time and the book of Genesis, and much of the last book is a long figurative reading of the days of creation. The last four days take what a first-time reader can follow, and say honestly where it is hard. We have taken thirteen passages, one from each book, about 2,500 words in all. The whole of the work, in this translation, is about 110,000 words.
The translation, the edition and the licence

The English in the passages is the translation of E. B. Pusey, who is named on the title page of the file as Edward Bouverie Pusey. Pusey was an Oxford churchman and scholar, and he died in 1882. Augustine and he are both long out of copyright, so the translation is in the public domain. It is available from Project Gutenberg as ebook number 3296, and every quotation in this book was checked against that text, word for word.

The file does not print a date for the translation. Pusey's version was first published in 1838, which is the year we give, and we cannot say which later printing the file follows. The file prints the thirteen headings BOOK I to BOOK XIII, but it does not number the chapters inside them, so every passage here is cited by Book alone. The words themselves will find it in any other edition.
What we changed in the passages is nothing. We kept the old spellings and the
Thou
Thee
and
Thy

, and the file's double hyphen where it stands for a dash. Where we skip a stretch inside a passage, a mark like this shows it: …. We quote only Augustine's text, never the headings, the header or the licence of the file. The choice and order of the passages, the reflections, the questions and the prayers are ours, and they are original.
Nothing of the Project Gutenberg licence text or trademark is copied here.
Where does a journey begin, if it is not in the feet that people leave and return?
The passage

paras.t: Thou awakest us to delight in Thy praise; for Thou madest us for Thyself, and our heart is restless, until it repose in Thee. … Passing hence from infancy, I came to boyhood, or rather it came to me, displacing infancy. Nor did that depart,--(for whither went it?)--and yet it was no more. … For it is not by our feet, or change of place, that men leave Thee, or return unto Thee. Or did that Thy younger son look out for horses or chariots, or ships, fly with visible wings, or journey by the motion of his limbs, that he might in a far country waste in riotous living all Thou gavest at his departure? a loving Father, when Thou gavest, and more loving unto him, when he returned empty.

spans.t: Reflection

On the first morning of a long walk, nearly everything can be counted. The kilometres to the first village. The litres of water. The weight of the pack, which you will feel in your shoulders within the hour and know to the gram by the end of the week. A walk is a countable thing, and there is comfort in that.
Augustine begins his book with something that cannot be counted. A few lines into the first page he says why anyone praises God at all, and the reason is one sentence long:
Thou madest us for Thyself, and our heart is restless, until it repose in Thee.
He is speaking to God, which is why the whole book says
Thou
. The sentence says that people are made for God, and that nothing smaller settles the heart. The book keeps coming back to it, and so does this one. The last day returns to the same word.

You do not have to pray to hear the other half of it. There is a restlessness in a good many of us that a better view, a bigger lunch or a finished day does not quite quiet. You may know it from the way a hand goes to the phone in the first still moment, or from the second coffee nobody wanted. Augustine does not treat it as a fault in the equipment. He treats it as a compass. That is a surprising way to open a confession. You might expect a list of failings. Instead the first thing he admits is a longing, and the first thing he says about himself is that he is not finished.

The second stretch of the passage turns, without warning, to his own early life. A few paragraphs earlier he has said that he remembers nothing of his infancy. He knows it only from what he was told and from watching other babies, and he is careful to say so. Now he writes:
Passing hence from infancy, I came to boyhood, or rather it came to me, displacing infancy.
Then comes a small, odd question in brackets:
for whither went it?

The infant is gone, and not gone. Each age of a life is pushed aside by the next and stays somewhere underneath. A long walk can stir them up. The tired child who wants to sit down at the next wall. The teenager who will not be seen to struggle. The grown-up with a plan. You may meet all three before lunch.
Third comes the sentence that a book for walkers has to stop for:
For it is not by our feet, or change of place, that men leave Thee, or return unto Thee.

His picture is the younger son in a story from the Gospel of Luke, which Augustine expects you to know. A young man takes his share of his father's money, goes off to a far country and spends it all, then comes home to a father who is glad to see him. Did the son need horses, chariots, ships or wings to get away, Augustine asks? He did not. The distance lay in what the son loved, not in how far he travelled, and the way home was the same.

It stings to read that on the first day of a walk of about 320 km. If distance is not in the feet, why lace the boots? The sentence does not say that walking is pointless. It says that walking cannot be all of it, and cannot do your returning for you. Feet are very good at moving a body to a place. They cannot carry the rest of you unless the rest of you is willing. Here is a fair doubt to set beside it. A body that is tired, away from its usual noise and out of reach of its usual chores, may be better placed to notice what is happening inside it than the same body at a desk. Augustine does not say so. The road might.

Where is the passage hard? Perhaps in its very first word of address. A reader who does not believe in a God to whom things can be said may feel shut out on the first page. The invitation is modest. Listen as you would to someone praying quietly in the next bunk. You need not join in. You can still hear what it sounds like to want something that much.

What might this change on an ordinary day? Something small. To bring the restlessness along instead of hiding it. To stop calling it a bad mood, and ask what it is reaching for. Over the coming days it will turn out to be reaching for a good deal: a crowd's approval, a lost friend, a clever teacher, a quiet window. For today it is enough to notice that it is there, and that you set out with it.
For the walk

items.t: What is restless in me this morning, and what am I reaching for to quiet it? Give the answer one honest word, even if the word is "coffee".

For the first ten minutes, notice each time your hand goes to a pocket for the phone, a snack or the map. Do not stop it, and do not scold it. Take one more step before you decide, and see whether the wish is still there when you arrive at the decision.

spans.t: At the end of the day
The boots are off, and your feet are making their case. Before the evening fills up with other things, give the day one look from the restless end.

Some of it was hard in the ordinary way. The pack argued with your shoulders. A stretch dragged. At some point the plan for the day and the body that had to carry it disagreed, and the body won. Name the hardest hour, plainly, and leave it there. It does not need mending tonight.
Some of it was good. It might have been a small thing: the first cold drink, a bell somewhere behind you, the plain pleasure of having gone a long way without a screen. Say that too.

Then think about the restlessness. Perhaps it eased as the day went on, as it often does when the body has something simple to do. Perhaps it only changed shape, from a wish to be somewhere else into a wish for a bed, a meal, a wash. That is a smaller restlessness than the one in the passage, but it is where an honest evening starts. There may also have been a moment when you saw what you were reaching for, and reached anyway. That is allowed. The aim of a first evening is only to have seen it once.

Your feet did their work today, and they deserve a mention. Augustine's sentence leaves a question that the evening is good for. Did the rest of you arrive where the feet did? Some days the body is in the village while the mind is still back at the last argument, or a step ahead at tomorrow's hill. That is not a failure. It is only worth noticing which part of you is in the room tonight.
And a small kindness for the child who walked with you. Whatever age turned up today, the tired one or the proud one, it did what it could. It is probably the one who most needs the bed.

If the restlessness is loud tonight, there is an old and plain remedy: do the next small thing. Rinse the socks. Fill the bottle. Write two lines to someone at home. Nothing in Augustine forbids a clean pair of socks. His book is stern in places, but its first pages are grateful for milk and warmth, and he says that he was received into life by
the comforts of woman's milk
. Nothing there is ashamed of needing things, and neither need you be.

A word for the tired. If the questions below slide off, let them. A restless heart and a tired body are not the same thing, and sleep is a perfectly good answer to the second. The questions will keep until morning, and so will the heart.

items.t: What did I reach for today when I was restless?
When, even for a minute, did I feel entirely where I was?
Which of my ages walked today: the child, the teenager or the grown-up?

spans.t: A short prayer

Tonight I am tired, and something in me is still not at rest. I will not pretend otherwise. Let the walking do what it can. Let sleep do the rest. Whatever it is I am looking for, let it be near. Let the morning find me willing to go on.
What do you do in company that you would never do alone?
The passage

paras.t: A pear tree there was near our vineyard, laden with fruit, tempting neither for colour nor taste. To shake and rob this, some lewd young fellows of us went, late one night (having according to our pestilent custom prolonged our sports in the streets till then), and took huge loads, not for our eating, but to fling to the very hogs, having only tasted them. And this, but to do what we liked only, because it was misliked. … Behold my God, before Thee, the vivid remembrance of my soul; alone, I had never committed that theft wherein what I stole pleased me not, but that I stole; nor had it alone liked me to do it, nor had I done it. O friendship too unfriendly! thou incomprehensible inveigler of the soul, thou greediness to do mischief out of mirth and wantonness, thou thirst of others' loss, without lust of my own gain or revenge: but when it is said, "Let's go, let's do it," we are ashamed not to be shameless.

spans.t: Reflection

It is two in the afternoon, and the sun sits on the back of your neck. The group ahead has just agreed to push on to the next village. Your legs had already agreed to stop at this one. You go on. Nobody asked you to, and nobody would have minded if you had stayed. Something in the air of a group did the asking.
That is a very mild form of what Augustine writes about in the second book of the
Confessions
, and his example is a theft of pears.
He is in his sixteenth year. There is a pear tree near the family vineyard, and the fruit is
tempting neither for colour nor taste

. Late one night, after hours of roaming the streets, a gang of lads shakes the tree and carries off great loads of pears. They do not eat them. They throw them to the pigs, having only tasted a few. The whole point, he says, was to do what they liked
because it was misliked

The detail that stays is the pigs. A crowd of young men, in the dark, shakes a tree for fruit they do not want and flings it to animals that will eat it without a word of thanks. It would be funny if he did not mean it so seriously.

What troubles him, decades later, is that there was no reason. People do wrong for money, for power, for revenge, out of fear, and he goes through the list in the pages around this one. None of it applied. He had better pears at home. He was not hungry. The fruit gave him no pleasure, and the only sweetness in it was the wrongdoing.
It was foul, and I loved it

, he says, which is about as blunt as a sentence can be. So he asks himself why he did it, which is the question that makes the passage worth reading. And he finds an answer he did not expect. It was the company.
alone, I had never committed that theft
, he writes, and then he turns on the very thing he valued most:
O friendship too unfriendly!
The line the whole day hangs on comes last:
but when it is said, "Let's go, let's do it," we are ashamed not to be shameless.
It is not wickedness that moves the lads, as he sees it. It is embarrassment. Nobody wants to be the one who says no.

Two doubts belong beside this. The first is proportion. To most readers now, a night of stolen fruit by teenage boys is small stuff, and the weight Augustine gives it can look out of scale. Much of the second book is built on it. He seems to choose a small wrong on purpose, one with no excuse of hunger or gain, so that he can look at something in himself without anything else in the way. You do not have to share his verdict to find his observation sound.

The second doubt is about who is speaking. The boy is seen by a bishop in his forties, who has had a long time to be hard on him. He is both the only witness and the prosecutor. Take the story as one man's portrait of himself, told in his own severe light, and hold the severity a little loosely.

The pull of a crowd does not only run towards harm. The instinct that makes a gang of lads shake a tree is the instinct that makes a table of strangers pass the bread along, or a whole group slow down for the one who is limping. Augustine is not telling you to distrust company. He is asking where it is carrying you, and whether you chose the direction.

A road with many walkers on it has a great many small crowds, forming and dissolving all day: the early start everyone seems to be making, the daily distance, the rumour of a good place to eat. Each one makes a decision within earshot of you. What does the passage ask of an ordinary day? Mostly attention to the small
let's go

moments, before they have finished happening. In each there is a half second in which you could ask whether you want this. You may find that you do. Being carried along is not automatically wrong. It is only unexamined until you have looked.
For the walk

items.t: Whose pace am I walking at today, and whose pace did I choose?

At the next decision the group makes, about where to stop, when to eat or how far to go, say to yourself what you want before you hear what anyone else wants. Then notice whether you say it aloud. If you are walking alone, the crowd may be in your head, in the walkers you passed yesterday and the pace you think you ought to keep. Notice that crowd too.

spans.t: At the end of the day
Pack straps leave marks that are faint and a little sore, and so do group decisions. The evening is when you find them. Look back over the day for the moments when a plan was made around you.

Some of those were good. A walker you had never met shortened a stretch so that you could keep up. Somebody made room at a crowded table. Nothing about being in company was a burden for an hour, and you may be a little surprised how warm that feels.

Some of them were hard. You went on when you needed to stop, or said yes to a drink you did not want, or laughed at a remark that sat badly. If you can find one, give it a name. You do not need to be hard on yourself about it. The boy in the passage has a grown man to be hard on him for everyone, and he does not need your help.

Then turn the question over, and look for the quieter half of Augustine's line. We are ashamed not to be shameless. Was there a moment today when you were a little ashamed to be decent? You might have swallowed a thank you because the mood was dry. You might have let a joke go past that you would have liked to answer. You might have wanted to ask the quiet walker to join the table, and not done it, because nobody else had. Those are the small pear trees. Nothing is stolen, and still something is lost.

Ask the other question too. Where did you pull someone else along today? You may have been the one who said that the next village was not far. You may have been the one who set a pace without asking whether it suited the others. A crowd is made of people, and today you were one of them.

One more look, and a kinder one. Think of the person whose company made the day lighter: the one who made you laugh at the wrong moment, or handed you a sweet at the right one. You need not know the name. A day with such a person in it is a good day, whatever else it held, and the passage is not an argument against them. It is only a reminder to notice what your company is doing to you, the way you notice what a new pair of boots is doing to your feet.

Honest tiredness is useful here. A tired body is easy to lead, and the afternoon's agreements were probably made with the least of you present. If that is true, tomorrow's first decision, made with a rested mind, is your chance to take one back.
Tomorrow the first
let's go
will arrive before breakfast is over. You do not have to say no to it. You only have to hear it, which is most of the work of choosing.

items.t: When did I say yes today because everyone else was saying it?
Where was I a little ashamed to be kind, and what did I do about it?
Whom did I carry along with me today, without asking?

spans.t: A short prayer

Tonight I thank you for the company I kept. Where it carried me well, let me remember it. Where I went along without choosing, forgive me, and help me choose tomorrow. Let me be someone who can say yes and no. Keep my feet honest and my mind awake.

chapters.title: Day 3. The son of these tears

spans.t: What can you do for someone you cannot reach?
The passage

paras.t: Thou gavest her then another answer, by a Priest of Thine, a certain Bishop brought up in Thy Church, and well studied in Thy books. … For he answered, that I was yet unteachable, being puffed up with the novelty of that heresy, and had already perplexed divers unskilful persons with captious questions, as she had told him: "but let him alone a while" (saith he), "only pray God for him, he will of himself by reading find what that error is, and how great its impiety." … Which when he had said, and she would not be satisfied, but urged him more, with entreaties and many tears, that he would see me and discourse with me; he, a little displeased at her importunity, saith, "Go thy ways and God bless thee, for it is not possible that the son of these tears should perish." Which answer she took (as she often mentioned in her conversations with me) as if it had sounded from heaven.

spans.t: Reflection

At the end of a day's walking there is often a phone, and on the phone there is often someone who is worried. Perhaps a message is waiting from a person at home who wants to know that you are safe. Perhaps you are the one composing a message you are not sure you should send, to someone whose choices you cannot stop thinking about. In both cases the distance is the same. There is a person you love, and there is a screen, and there is not much more that you can do.
The third book of the
Confessions

has a mother in that position. She is Augustine's mother, whom the book names only once, at the very end of the ninth book, as Monnica. The usual spelling is Monica. He is a young man in Carthage, and he has joined a religious movement of his day called the Manichees. He stays with it for about nine years. The details of what the Manichees taught do not matter for today. What matters is that his mother thinks he is lost, and cannot make him listen.

She had already been given a dream, just before this in the book. She stood weeping on a wooden rule, and a shining young man asked her why. When she said that she was mourning her son, he told her to look, and there he was, standing beside her on the same rule. Augustine, when she told him, tried to bend it to another meaning: that she should not despair of becoming what he was. She answered at once that the dream had said no such thing. It had said that where she was, he would be also. She did not give way on that, and she was right to notice what the sentence said.
So she goes to a bishop. Augustine does not name him. He is
well studied in Thy books
, and she begs him to talk to her son, to argue with him and set him right. The bishop says no. Augustine, writing long afterwards, adds
wisely, as I afterwards perceived

. The young man, the bishop tells her, is not yet teachable. He is excited by his new ideas and has been catching out less skilled people with clever questions. Arguing with him now would only make him dig in.
Then comes the advice:
let him alone a while.

Pray for him, the bishop says. Reading will show him the error in time. The bishop knows what he is talking about. He says that he too was handed over to the Manichees as a boy by his own mother, that he read and copied their books, and that he saw for himself, with nobody arguing him out of it, that he must leave. She will not be put off, and keeps asking
with entreaties and many tears
. At last he answers, a little displeased at her importunity, as Augustine candidly says.
Go thy ways and God bless thee, for it is not possible that the son of these tears should perish.
The most hopeful sentence in the story was said by a man who was a little put out at being pressed. She took it, Augustine says,
as if it had sounded from heaven.
There are two places where this is hard. The first is the advice itself.
Let him alone

can sound like giving up. It is not quite that. The bishop is not telling her to stop caring. He is telling her to stop arguing, and to keep praying. What he asks of her is patience, and trust that the young man has a road of his own to walk. Even a reader who does not pray may know that some people cannot be talked out of a position they have just taken up, and that the talking only hardens it.

The second is the last sentence. Augustine tells the story long after it ended well. He knows the result, and so the bishop's words come to him as a prophecy. Not every story ends that way, and a mother's tears are love, not a guarantee. If you are carrying someone whose road has not turned, the line may sting. Take it as the comfort it was to her on that day, and not as a promise anyone can be held to.

What does that leave for today? If you are the worried one, perhaps one small release: to do what you can, which may only be a kind message that asks for nothing, and then to let the person be, for a while. If you are the one being worried about, the story offers something too. Somewhere behind you, there may be someone who has worried for you in silence. You do not have to repay it today. You could let them know that you are well.
For the walk

items.t: Who am I trying to change at the moment, and what would it be to leave that person alone for an hour?

Choose one person, near or far, whom you have wanted to correct or fix. For the rest of the morning, do not rehearse the argument. Each time it begins, wish them well in one short sentence, and walk on.
If nobody comes to mind, think of yourself. What are you pushing against in your own body or mind this morning that might do better left alone for an hour?

spans.t: At the end of the day

Evenings are when the messages arrive. If one is waiting, read it slowly. If you can answer in one kind line, do. A short "I am well, thank you for thinking of me" has been a great comfort to a great many people, and it costs a minute.

Look back at the day through the bishop's advice. Notice first who, today, said something to you that you took in precisely because they did not press it: a fellow walker who told you one thing about their own mistakes and then let it lie. That is how the bishop dealt with her. He told his own story once, and left it. Was there someone you wanted to set right? It might have been a companion who gave a wrong direction with great confidence, or someone whose view of the world you could not let pass. Perhaps you said what you thought and it did not help. Perhaps you held it in, and found that holding it in was easier than you expected. Either way, notice how it felt to want to correct someone and not do it. That is the practice the bishop was asking for.

Think too of the opposite person, the one who has been letting you alone. A friend who did not push when you were short with them. A partner who did not ask the question you would have snapped at. They are often easy to miss, because what they give is an absence. Tonight you could be glad of one such absence.

If today brought news that worries you, be honest that the evening is the worst time to think about it. Tired minds make small problems large. Nothing you decide at this hour will be your best decision. Write down the worry if that helps, in a line, and leave it on the page. The bishop's advice is not to forget the person. It is to put the matter down for the night and trust the morning to hold it.

Keep the length of the road in proportion, too. Augustine's nine years were a long time, and a road of about two weeks is short beside them. It may stir something. It will not finish anything. That is no failure of the road, and no failure of yours.

And a word about the tiredness that comes after emotional days. You may find that you are more tired than the distance explains. Worry is heavy and carries no weight on a scale. A long hot wash, a cup of something, an early night: these count as help. Nobody on earth is served by a walker who sits up rehearsing a conversation.

If there is nobody to message tonight, that is also a fact of the road, and no failure. A kind thought sent without a message is a small and private act, and nobody is owed more than that at this hour.

items.t: Whom did I try to change today, and what happened in me when I held back?
Who may be thinking of me tonight, and have I let them know that I am well?
What would it be to wait with someone instead of working on them?

spans.t: A short prayer

Tonight I think of the people I cannot reach. Keep them, and let them know they are loved. Where I have been pushing, teach me to wait. Where I have been waited for, give me the grace to answer. Let me sleep, and trust the morning to carry what I cannot.

chapters.title: Day 4. A great riddle to myself

spans.t: Where do you take a sorrow that goes everywhere you go?
The passage

paras.t: At this grief my heart was utterly darkened; and whatever I beheld was death. My native country was a torment to me, and my father's house a strange unhappiness; and whatever I had shared with him, wanting him, became a distracting torture. Mine eyes sought him every where, but he was not granted them; and I hated all places, for that they had not him; nor could they now tell me, "he is coming," as when he was alive and absent. I became a great riddle to myself, and I asked my soul, why she was so sad, and why she disquieted me sorely: but she knew not what to answer me. And if I said, Trust in God, she very rightly obeyed me not; because that most dear friend, whom she had lost, was, being man, both truer and better than that phantasm she was bid to trust in. Only tears were sweet to me, for they succeeded my friend, in the dearest of my affections. … For I bore about a shattered and bleeding soul, impatient of being borne by me, yet where to repose it, I found not. … For whither should my heart flee from my heart? Whither should I flee from myself? Whither not follow myself? And yet I fled out of my country; for so should mine eyes less look for him, where they were not wont to see him.

spans.t: Reflection

People walk the Camino for many reasons, and grief is one of them. It travels in the pack with the water and the spare socks, and it does not get lighter at the top of a hill. Perhaps you are carrying one. Perhaps the person on the next bench is, and you will never know. Either way, today's reading is for them.
In the fourth book of the
Confessions

, Augustine is a young teacher in his home town, and he has a friend. They grew up together, as school-fellows and play-fellows, and for a year or so the friendship has been the sweetest thing in his life. Then the friend falls ill with a fever and dies. Augustine was away when it happened.
What follows is some of the plainest writing about grief in any old book.
At this grief my heart was utterly darkened; and whatever I beheld was death.
His own town becomes a torment. His father's house is a strange unhappiness. He hates every place
for that they had not him
, and the places cannot even say what they used to say, that his friend is coming soon. Notice how small the details are. Grief in this passage is mostly a matter of eyes that keep looking at doors.
Then the line that gives the day its title:
I became a great riddle to myself.
He asks his soul why it is so sad, and it has no answer. He tells it to trust in God, and the soul, as he puts it,
very rightly obeyed me not.

This is worth a pause. A consolation offered too early, even to oneself, is not an answer, and Augustine is honest enough to say that his soul was right to refuse it. The friend, a real person, was truer and better than the vague, shapeless God he then had to trust in, which Augustine later calls a phantom. The only thing he found sweet was crying.

If you carry no such sorrow, the passage is still worth keeping, because it tells you how not to be a companion. A person in grief may not need to be told to trust in anything, not at first. A walker beside you who is quiet and keeps pace, and says very little, may be doing the kindest thing on the road.
In the second stretch he looks for rest, and the verb he uses will mean something to anyone who has carried a pack:
I bore about a shattered and bleeding soul, impatient of being borne by me.

He is carrying himself, and he is impatient of the weight. He tried the usual remedies. The passage skips the list, but it is there in the text: groves, games and music, banquets, books. Nothing took the load.
So, in the last stretch, he does what a good many people have done.
And yet I fled out of my country; for so should mine eyes less look for him, where they were not wont to see him.
He left for Carthage. Before that, though, comes the question that is the best thing in the passage:
For whither should my heart flee from my heart?

You cannot walk away from the one who is walking. In the pages that follow, time and other friends patch him up, little by little. He does not call that a cure. He goes on to ask why the grief reached him so far in the first place.

Two limits are worth stating. The passage offers no consolation, and you will not find one in it. Augustine finds an answer of his own a few pages later, and it belongs to his faith. It need not be handed to anyone today. And a walk will not mend every sorrow. If what you carry is heavier than a road can lighten, tell somebody: a friend, a doctor, a counsellor, a helpline in your own country. In Spain, 112 is the emergency number for anything that cannot wait.

What is an ordinary day to do with all this? Very little. It gives leave to be a riddle to yourself. It gives leave to cry, and equally leave not to, if the tears do not come. And it suggests a small change in the way you walk with the weight. Not to flee, which he tried, and not to wrestle, but to let it walk beside you, and to put it down, now and then, on a bench.
For the walk

items.t: What am I carrying that I cannot put down yet? Could it walk beside me today, rather than in front?

At a place where the path turns, say the name of someone you miss, silently or aloud. Do not try to feel anything in particular. Then walk on. If no name comes, say the name of someone you are glad of. At your next rest, take the pack off slowly and notice the moment when its weight leaves your shoulders. Let that be the whole practice.

spans.t: At the end of the day
Some evenings the body is quiet and the heart is not. If today was one of those, sit for a while with the lights low and let the day arrive.

You may have cried, in a field or a bathroom or a corner of the dormitory, with a hand over your mouth. That is allowed, and a long road has room for it. Or the tears may not have come, and you walked all day as if through glass. That is allowed too. Nothing in the passage says you must feel on schedule, and Augustine himself did not know what he felt: he calls himself a riddle.

Think of the places in the day that had a gap in them, like the doors in the passage. A seat across from you that nobody filled. A joke you wanted to tell someone. A view you would have liked to show to one person in particular. These are the small doors. You do not have to explain them to anyone. You only have to notice that you looked.

Think also of what was good, because grief is not the whole of any day. A mouthful of something hot. A kindness that arrived from nowhere. A moment in which you forgot, and then remembered, and found you could bear the remembering. If a good moment feels like a betrayal of the one you miss, you may have it anyway. In the very next paragraph after the first stretch, Augustine says that
time hath assuaged my wound
, a sentence written from the far side of the sorrow, and you are allowed to arrive at it in your own time.

Grief is hard work, and it is the sort of work that does not show on a map. If you are more worn out tonight than the distance can explain, this is why. Be gentle with yourself about the pace. Wash, eat something plain, and let the body have what it asks for. A friend, a call, a cup of tea, a very early night: all of these are good company for a sorrow. You are not behind in anything.
If you were beside someone else's sorrow today, perhaps without being told, think about what you did. Did you fill the silence, or share it? Often the whole help is in staying at the same pace.

If you did tell someone today how things really are, however briefly, notice what it was like. If you did not, ask whether there is someone you could tell tomorrow. And if a church door is open on tomorrow's road, a candle is a gentle thing to light for the one you miss, whatever you believe. It is a small and quiet way of saying a name.
Before you sleep, say the name once if you wish, and say nothing if you would rather. The night will keep it either way.

items.t: Who did I miss today, and what did I do with the missing?
Where did I try to outwalk something, and what happened when I stopped?
Who could I tell tonight, or tomorrow, how the day really was?

spans.t: A short prayer

Tonight I bring the one I miss. I do not know what to say, so I will simply sit. Let the sorrow be allowed to be here. Let the day's small kindnesses be enough for tonight. Hold what I cannot carry, and let me sleep.

chapters.title: Day 5. How he spoke, and what he said

spans.t: When someone speaks well, what are you listening to?
The passage

paras.t: But what availed the utmost neatness of the cup-bearer to my thirst for a more precious draught? Mine ears were already cloyed with the like, nor did they seem to me therefore better, because better said; nor therefore true, because eloquent; nor the soul therefore wise, because the face was comely, and the language graceful. … For he was not altogether ignorant of his own ignorance, nor would he rashly be entangled in a dispute, whence he could neither retreat nor extricate himself fairly. Even for this I liked him the better. For fairer is the modesty of a candid mind, than the knowledge of those things which I desired; and such I found him, in all the more difficult and subtile questions. … That man of God received me as a father, and showed me an Episcopal kindness on my coming. Thenceforth I began to love him, at first indeed not as a teacher of the truth (which I utterly despaired of in Thy Church), but as a person kind towards myself. … And while I opened my heart to admit "how eloquently he spake," there also entered "how truly he spake"; but this by degrees.

spans.t: Reflection

Anyone who has been truly thirsty knows that the beauty of the cup is not the point. A glass can be cut with great care and polished until it sings, and if it is empty you are still thirsty. Augustine uses exactly this picture in the fifth book of the
Confessions

For nearly nine years he had belonged to the Manichees, the movement he joined in his nineteenth year, and for most of that time he had been carrying questions the local teachers could not answer. They all said the same thing: wait for Faustus. Faustus was a bishop of their movement, a famous speaker, and when he came to Carthage the questions would be answered. Augustine longed for that visit, he says, rather too intensely, and when Faustus finally arrived he turned out to be pleasant, fluent and graceful, and to say
the self-same things
as everyone else.
That is where the cup-bearer comes in:
what availed the utmost neatness of the cup-bearer to my thirst for a more precious draught?

The words did not seem to him better because they were better said. They did not seem true because they were eloquent. The soul was not wise because the face was comely. It is a hard lesson to hold on to in a world of good presenters, and anyone who has been swept along by a confident voice, in a kitchen or on a screen, will know how easily the cup can be mistaken for the water.

Here is the surprise of the passage. Having lost his hopes in Faustus, Augustine does not turn on him. He gives him credit. When Augustine put his hard questions, Faustus did not bluster. He knew his limits. Faustus, Augustine says,
was not altogether ignorant of his own ignorance
, and would not walk into an argument he could not get out of.
Even for this I liked him the better.
A teacher who says that he does not know is rarer than one who says a great deal, and Augustine saw it. The passage ends the story of a letdown with a small piece of respect.
Then the road moves to Milan. Augustine has come to teach, and there he meets the bishop, Ambrose. Ambrose receives him
as a father
. Augustine does not begin by loving the teaching. He begins by loving a person who was kind to him,
not as a teacher of the truth
, he says, since he had given up on finding truth in Ambrose's church,
but as a person kind towards myself
. He goes to hear the sermons only to judge the style, to see whether the famous eloquence lived up to its name. Of the content he was
a careless and scornful looker-on
. And then comes the best sentence in the passage:
And while I opened my heart to admit "how eloquently he spake," there also entered "how truly he spake"; but this by degrees.
Notice what Augustine remembers about that first meeting. Not a word of what Ambrose said. He remembers how he was received:
an Episcopal kindness on my coming

. A bishop with a great many calls on his time made room for a stranger who had been sent to teach in his city, and treated him as if he mattered. The teaching came later. The welcome came first, and it may be the reason the teaching was heard at all.

It is a very gentle account of changing one's mind. No argument defeats him. He went for the style, and the meaning came in beside it, a little at a time, through a door he had left open for another purpose.

There is a fair doubt to raise. Taken alone, that sentence could describe how people drift into anything, good or bad. Being moved by a speaker proves nothing about what the speaker says, and Augustine knows it. The lines just after the first stretch, which we have left out, make the point at length. Eloquence does not prove something true, and plainness does not prove it false. So the sentence is not a recommendation to follow whoever moves you. It is an observation about how slowly and sideways the truth, if it comes, tends to come.

Put to work on an ordinary day, this means listening in two ways. Once for the manner: the accent, the humour, the confidence, the warmth. Once for the matter: what, in plain words, was actually said. And to notice whom you trust because of kindness before you have heard a word of their argument. On a road with a great many conversations in it, at tables and in doorways, there is plenty of practice to be had.
For the walk

items.t: Who has spoken to me well lately, and what did they actually say?

In your next conversation, listen once for how it is said and once for what is said. At the end, give yourself the "what" in one plain sentence. If the sentence will not come, that is worth knowing too. If you are walking alone, try the same with the next thing you read: a sign, a message, a headline. What did it say, once the tone has been taken away?

spans.t: At the end of the day

Conversations leave a residue, like the salt on a shirt. By the evening you may not remember a single thing anyone said, only that you liked them, or did not. That is not a failure of memory. It is the first half of Augustine's lesson, the part that happens before the meaning arrives.

Go back through the day's talk, as far as you can reach. Who spoke well? Not necessarily the loudest. Perhaps a man at a table who told a story that held the room. Perhaps a woman who said very little, and said it exactly. Try to remember what they said, not only how they said it. Some of it will have gone. Some of it will have stayed, and you may be surprised which.

Then ask the harder question. Was there anything you accepted today because of the way it was said? A confident view on the weather, the route, the right way to pack a bag, a person's character, the state of the world. Confidence is often borrowed, and most of us lend it on trust. There is no need to go back and unpick all of it tonight. It is enough to notice that you took some of it on credit.

Think also of how you were received today, because that is Ambrose's half of the lesson. A greeting at a door. A hand pointing out the right bunk. A word of welcome from someone who owed you nothing. It is easy to forget these within an hour, and it is a pity, because they are often the true beginning of whatever the road is teaching you. Augustine never forgot his, and wrote it down sixteen centuries ago.

And think of Faustus, because he is the friendlier figure in the passage. He did something rare and slightly brave. When he did not know, he said so, and the man he disappointed liked him better for it. Did you have a chance today to say that you did not know? Did you take it? If you did not, that was probably a small relief at the time. But it is worth remembering how the sentence is received by someone who is listening for the truth.

One small practice for tonight, if you have the energy. Take the last conversation you had, and listen to it again in memory, twice: once for the way it was said, once for what was said. You will not hear the second the first time.

Tiredness, honestly: a tired mind is easy to persuade, and may nod at anything offered with a smile. If tonight you read a message, a headline or a rumour and nodded along, give it a night before you decide what you think.

items.t: Whose words did I take in today without weighing them?
Who was kind to me before I knew what they had to give?
When did I say that I did not know, or wish that I had?

spans.t: A short prayer

Tonight I am grateful for the voices of the day. Let me hear what is true under what is only pleasant. Keep me grateful to the kind people who are not impressive. Teach me to say that I do not know when I do not. Let slow truth come in, a little at a time, and let me not run from it.

chapters.title: Day 6. The man who read in silence

spans.t: What do you do when the person you need has no time for you?
The passage

paras.t: But when he was reading, his eye glided over the pages, and his heart searched out the sense, but his voice and tongue were at rest. Ofttimes when we had come (for no man was forbidden to enter, nor was it his wont that any who came should be announced to him), we saw him thus reading to himself, and never otherwise; and having long sat silent (for who durst intrude on one so intent?) we were fain to depart, conjecturing that in the small interval which he obtained, free from the din of others' business, for the recruiting of his mind, he was loth to be taken off; and perchance he dreaded lest if the author he read should deliver any thing obscurely, some attentive or perplexed hearer should desire him to expound it, or to discuss some of the harder questions; so that his time being thus spent, he could not turn over so many volumes as he desired; although the preserving of his voice (which a very little speaking would weaken) might be the truer reason for his reading to himself. But with what intent soever he did it, certainly in such a man it was good. … I however certainly had no opportunity of enquiring what I wished of that so holy oracle of Thine, his breast, unless the thing might be answered briefly. But those tides in me, to be poured out to him, required his full leisure, and never found it.

spans.t: Reflection

Somewhere on every road there is a doorway with a queue in it. Behind the door is someone who could answer the one question you have been carrying for days, and between you and them is a crowd of people with questions of their own. You get as far as the threshold, see how things are, and sit down to wait. After a while you find you have been waiting a long time and your question has not got any smaller.

That is Augustine in Milan, and the person behind the door is Ambrose, the city's bishop. He has come to the city to teach. He wants to talk to Ambrose about the things that trouble him, and he cannot. The bishop is, as Augustine puts it, shut off by
multitudes of busy people, whose weaknesses he served
. Whenever Ambrose is not with them, he is eating what the body needs, or he is reading.

Augustine writes the scene carefully, as someone who watched it more than once. Nobody was forbidden to enter, and visitors were not even announced. You simply walked in and found him with a book. Augustine describes it exactly:
his eye glided over the pages, and his heart searched out the sense, but his voice and tongue were at rest.
He was reading to himself, with no sound. Augustine and the others would sit for a long time,
for who durst intrude on one so intent?
, and then slip away.

It clearly struck Augustine as worth explaining, because he offers three guesses. Perhaps Ambrose wanted a quiet stretch to rest his mind away from the din of other people's business. Perhaps he did not want a puzzled listener to ask him to explain a hard line aloud. Perhaps he simply wished to save his voice, which a little speaking would tire. Then comes the best sentence in the passage:
But with what intent soever he did it, certainly in such a man it was good.
He does not know which reason is true. He decides to think well of the man whichever it is.
The second stretch is plain frustration. He had
no opportunity of enquiring
what he wished from
that so holy oracle of Thine, his breast
, unless the question could be answered briefly. But the tides in him
required his full leisure, and never found it
. The image is good: a seeker with a sea of questions in him, and a teacher who has only a few minutes at a time.

Two things deserve a second look. The first is the generosity itself. Augustine reads Ambrose kindly because he has already decided to admire him. Would he have been as kind to a man he did not like, who sat silent behind a book and kept him waiting? It is easier to be generous to people we have already put on a shelf marked good. That is not a reason to give the generosity up. It is a reason to try it on someone harder.

The second doubt is about the ending. The passage does not tell you that waiting is rewarded. Augustine does not get his private conversation here. He gets something else, which he mentions in the next lines: he hears Ambrose preach to the people every Sunday, and over time he grows more sure that the objections he had met could be answered. The help arrives sideways, in public, to a crowd he happens to be part of. What you cannot get alone, you sometimes get as one of many. That is a comfort, but a small and unpredictable one.

On a plain day it asks for a little patience at the door of someone's time. And a habit of generous reading, where it costs nothing: the walker who strides ahead without a word, the host who has no time to chat, the stranger who answers shortly. They may be tired, or shy, or saving their voice. You do not need to know which. You can decide, as Augustine did, to think well of them whichever it is.
A small extra, for fun. Read the passage once more with your own lips and tongue at rest, the way he saw it done. You may hear it differently.
For the walk

items.t: Whose silence am I judging this morning? What are three kind reasons for it?

For the first stretch of the day, walk without starting a conversation. If you have a question you want answered by someone, let it wait unasked. Notice what the question does while it waits. Does it shrink, or sharpen, or turn into a different question? If a quiet moment comes later, you might also read something short with your lips at rest, and see what the eyes alone can take in.

spans.t: At the end of the day

A room full of tired people has its own way of going quiet. Lamps are clicked off, one at a time. Someone turns a page. Someone eases a zip along a millimetre at a time. Somewhere in the room there is probably a person who would love a conversation and is not going to have one. Perhaps it is you.

Look back at the day for the doors. Where did you have to wait? A queue for the kitchen, a long hour before a place opened, a walker you hoped to catch up with, a person you hoped to reach by phone and could not. Waiting is one of the plain facts of the road, and it is rarely mentioned in the pictures. What was it like, today? Did you fill it, or just sit through it?

Think about the people who were busy on your behalf. Whoever checked a great many walkers in, found beds, answered the same question many times over, kept the kitchen going. Augustine's Ambrose was surrounded by
multitudes of busy people, whose weaknesses he served

. It is easy to feel that such a person is unavailable to you. It is also true that they are available to everybody, and that you are one of a crowd that they are serving. If someone was short with you today, you could ask whether that was the tide going out.

Now turn to the silences. Whose did you misread today? A short answer, a face turned away, a quiet that seemed cold. Think of the guesses that come to mind first, and try giving each one a kinder twin. He was saving his voice. She was tired. He was shy. It will not always be true. It is a good habit even so, and it is gentler to sleep on.

If there was a stretch today in which you were quiet yourself, whether by choice or from fatigue, ask what it held. You may find, after a few days on a long road, that silence is less of an absence than it looked.

One last small kindness is worth the trouble. If there is somebody who has been quiet all day, near you, give them the smallest greeting before the lights go: a nod, a good night, a pass of the water bottle. You do not have to pull a conversation out of them. Augustine and his friends sat in Ambrose's room and left without a word, and he remembers it with respect, not resentment. A shared silence can be a way of keeping company.

Tiredness has a gift tonight. When you are very tired, you stop trying to make conversation, and a good deal of the effort drops away. Allow it. You are not being rude. You are being, for a while, a person who reads without a sound.

items.t: Whose silence did I read badly today, and what might be a kinder reading?
What question did I carry that needed more time than anyone had?
Where did I find even a minute of real quiet, and what did I do with it?

spans.t: A short prayer

Tonight I thank you for the people who made room for me, and for the ones who had none. Teach me to wait at a door without bitterness. Let me read the quiet of others generously. Let my own silence be rest and not retreat. Let my questions keep until they are ready to be answered.

chapters.title: Day 7. A glimpse and a road

spans.t: What do you do after the view?
The passage

paras.t: And being thence admonished to return to myself, I entered even into my inward self, Thou being my Guide: and able I was, for Thou wert become my Helper. And I entered and beheld with the eye of my soul (such as it was), above the same eye of my soul, above my mind, the Light Unchangeable. … And I wondered that I now loved Thee, and no phantasm for Thee. And yet did I not press on to enjoy my God; but was borne up to Thee by Thy beauty, and soon borne down from Thee by mine own weight, sinking with sorrow into these inferior things. … But I could not fix my gaze thereon; and my infirmity being struck back, I was thrown again on my wonted habits, carrying along with me only a loving memory thereof, and a longing for what I had, as it were, perceived the odour of, but was not yet able to feed on.

spans.t: Reflection

If the weather is kind, a mountain road will sooner or later give you a view. The cloud lifts, or the trees thin, and for a few minutes a whole country lies open below you: ridges folded behind ridges, a river somewhere, the line of a road you cannot yet walk. You stop. You may stand there for a good while. Then you shoulder the pack and go down into the next valley, and within the hour you are in a lane between hedges, and the view is a thing that happened.
The seventh book of the
Confessions
is about a view of that kind, and what became of it.

Augustine is about thirty and still searching. He has left the Manichees and is not yet sure what to believe. The book tells us that he has read certain books of the Platonists, philosophers in the tradition of Plato, in a Latin translation. They turn him away from the outside of things.
And being thence admonished to return to myself, I entered even into my inward self
, he says. And there, with what he calls
the eye of my soul
, above his own mind, he sees
the Light Unchangeable
Notice, too, how he got there. Nothing in the passage is a climb. It begins with a turn,
to return to myself

, and what follows is received rather than achieved. On a mountain road the same is true in a plain way. Two walkers can go up the same slope, one into clear air and one into cloud, and what each sees is not theirs to arrange.

This is the first day on which the passage may stretch you. He does not tell us what he saw. He tells us what it was not: it was not ordinary light, and not a stronger kind of ordinary light. If you cannot picture it, nothing has gone wrong with you. He could not, either, and says so by the way he writes. The part of the passage anyone can follow comes next.
It happens at once. He
was borne up to Thee by Thy beauty, and soon borne down from Thee by mine own weight
. He is lifted, and then he is let down, sinking with sorrow, as he puts it, into the ordinary things of life. The word to keep is
weight
. It returns on the last day of this book, with a different meaning.
And then the best image in the passage.
I could not fix my gaze thereon
, he says. He was thrown back on his old habits, and what he kept was
a loving memory thereof, and a longing for what I had, as it were, perceived the odour of, but was not yet able to feed on.

He smelled the meal and could not yet eat it. Nearly everyone who has walked past a kitchen on a hungry evening knows the exact feeling. A smell like that is not a feast, and it is a great deal more than nothing. It tells you where the food is, and keeps you walking.
A few pages after our passage, Augustine puts the whole thing in one sentence about a mountain:
from the mountain's shaggy top to see the land of peace, and to find no way thither.

He is thinking of the Platonist books, which showed him the goal clearly and did not show him the road. For him the road lay elsewhere, in the Christian faith and in what he calls humility, and he goes on to say so. This is a Christian book, and we say so plainly. But the sentence works on any hill. A view is not a route. To see where you are going is one thing. To find the path down, round and up again is another.

Two doubts, then. First, the vision is hard to share. Many religious traditions describe moments of this kind, and a reader who has never had one may feel shut out, or suspicious. Both are fair. Augustine does not ask you to have one. What he describes next is more widely shared: a high moment, and the return of the ordinary. Second, he is hard on the ordinary. To him, the pull back into old habits is a sorrow. You may think differently, and a good meal and a warm bed are not a failure of vision. Hold that part loosely.

What does a plain day need from all this? To expect the descent, and not read it as a defeat. And to look after what the view leaves you with. Not the view itself, which cannot be kept, but the loving memory and the longing: a good thing remembered, and a hunger for more of it. They are enough to walk on.
For the walk

items.t: What did I glimpse once that I could not hold? Is the longing still doing its work?

At the next open view, stop and look for a full minute, until it has gone a little ordinary. You will feel the moment. Then walk on and see that you can leave it behind, and that something comes with you. If today has no view in it, try the same with the next good thing instead: a shaded bench, a cold tap, a long stretch of sun on a wall.

spans.t: At the end of the day

Most days have a high point and a low one, and in the evening it is worth finding both. Without hurry, go through the day as you might scroll back through a road: the places where you were lifted, and the places where you were let down.

What lifted you? It might have been a view, as in the passage. It might have been a small kindness, a good song in your head, the second wind that arrives after a long climb. Be specific. A good thing named is easier to keep than a good thing left vague.

What pulled you down? It might have been a stretch of road, an ache, a thought that came uninvited at four o'clock. Augustine says he was borne down by his own weight. On a long walk the phrase is almost literal. You are heavier at the end of the day than at the beginning, and your thoughts are heavier with you. Part of what pulled you down may simply have been the hour.

Then ask what you kept. If the best part of today has already faded, as it nearly always does, is there still something left of it, like the smell of bread in a coat? A remembered light on a hillside. The sound of a river you passed. A hunger to see something like it again. That is the loving memory and the longing, and it is more than you might think.

If you shared a view today, there is a small gift in remembering that you saw it together. In this passage Augustine's glimpse is entirely his own, and it is a lonelier thing for it. Yours need not be.

Be honest, too, about the days when there was no view. Some days are wet and low, and the distance is the only thing on offer. They count. The passage does not say that only the high days are the real ones. It says that high moments pass, and the road goes on.

If a view did give you a clear sight of something, a kinder way of being, a conversation you have put off, a rest you need, here is the practical use of Augustine's mountain. A view is not a route, so choose the smallest step towards it that you can take tomorrow before noon, and fix it in your mind tonight. A step is a modest thing. It is also what is left when the view has gone, and it is the thing that can actually be walked.
If you cannot think what lifted you today, think instead of what carried you: a pair of socks, a warm drink, a bed with a blanket. A great deal of life is carried by small things.

If today included a long descent, your knees may have something to say. Take the ache seriously and tomorrow's downhill slowly, and ask a doctor or a pharmacist about any pain that does not ease. A road is long, and the body is the only one you have.

items.t: What lifted me today, and what pulled me down?
What have I kept from the best hour of today?
What am I hungry for tonight?

spans.t: A short prayer

Tonight I thank you for whatever lifted me, and for whatever carried me when I was low. Let me keep the memory of the good hour, and the longing that comes with it. Do not let me mistake a view for the road. Show me the next step, and let it be a small one. Let me sleep.
What are you putting off until tomorrow?
The passage

paras.t: For I said with myself, "Be it done now, be it done now." And as I spake, I all but enacted it: I all but did it, and did it not: yet sunk not back to my former state, but kept my stand hard by, and took breath. … I cast myself down I know not how, under a certain fig-tree, giving full vent to my tears; and the floods of mine eyes gushed out an acceptable sacrifice to Thee. … So was I speaking and weeping in the most bitter contrition of my heart, when, lo! I heard from a neighbouring house a voice, as of boy or girl, I know not, chanting, and oft repeating, "Take up and read; Take up and read." Instantly, my countenance altered, I began to think most intently whether children were wont in any kind of play to sing such words: nor could I remember ever to have heard the like. So checking the torrent of my tears, I arose; interpreting it to be no other than a command from God to open the book, and read the first chapter I should find. … No further would I read; nor needed I: for instantly at the end of this sentence, by a light as it were of serenity infused into my heart, all the darkness of doubt vanished away.

spans.t: Reflection

At the foot of a long climb there is a moment when you say, quietly, right, now. You look up at the slope. You adjust a strap. You take a drink you do not need. Then you say it again, and a minute has gone, and your feet have not moved. Nobody is watching, and nothing is wrong with your legs. It is the smallest version of a very old difficulty.
The eighth book of the
Confessions

is the book of that difficulty, at the largest size. By now Augustine has been searching for years. He has read, listened, doubted and half agreed, and in this book he sits in the little garden of his lodging with his friend Alypius, and something has to be decided. In the pages before the passage he tries to say what is happening in him, and the sentence he finds is one of the best in the book:
The mind commands the mind, its own self, to will, and yet it doth not.
A hand will move when it is told. A will does not always move when it is told, because part of it is willing and part is not. He calls it
partly to will, partly to nill
, and says it is a sort of sickness of the mind. Anyone who has ever meant to begin something and not begun it knows what he means.
The passage opens in the middle of the struggle.
Be it done now, be it done now
, he says to himself, and then:
I all but did it, and did it not.
He gets close to the edge and stops, but he does not go back either. In his words, he
kept my stand hard by, and took breath
. That is almost funny, and entirely true. Most of what we call putting something off is exactly this: standing close to the edge, breathing.
He goes away from Alypius to be alone, and throws himself down under a fig tree, and weeps. Then comes the oddest moment in the book. From a house nearby he hears a voice,
as of boy or girl, I know not
, singing over and over:
Take up and read; Take up and read.

He tries to think whether children chant such words in any game, and cannot remember that they do. So he takes it as a command to open the book that he has left lying by Alypius, which holds the letters of the apostle Paul, and to read the first passage his eyes fall on.
The passage then skips the lines that he reads, and it is right that you should know what they are. They are a few sentences of Paul, which Augustine copies out. They begin
Not in rioting and drunkenness
, they list behaviour to leave behind, and they end by telling the reader to
put ye on the Lord Jesus Christ
. He does not read on.
No further would I read; nor needed I.
At the end of the sentence, he says, a light of calm came into his heart and
all the darkness of doubt vanished away

Two things in this are hard. The first is the struggle itself. In the pages before the passage, what Augustine fights is mostly desire and the habits of a life he wants to leave, understood in the terms of a fourth-century Christian, and it is not a language that many readers share. We have kept to the part everyone can recognise: the divided will, the delay and the turning. If the rest sits badly with you, you are not alone and need not argue with him about it.

The second is the voice and the book. It is easy to hear this as a conjuring trick: a child's song, a page opened at random, a life changed. Nobody should settle a life by opening a book at a chance place, and Augustine does not. The scene comes at the end of years. He is also not sure where the voice came from. All he says is that he could not remember a game with such words. What changes him is not the verse as such. It is that he had been ready for a long time, and something finally gave him a reason to stop standing at the edge.

On an ordinary day, this comes down to something very small. The task is to find what you are all but doing, name it, and then look for its smallest piece. Not the whole of the matter. A message to be written, a number to look up, a hard word to be said to a person at home. And look, too, at who is sitting beside you. Alypius waited, in silence, close by, while his friend struggled. That counts for more than it seems.
For the walk

items.t: What am I all but doing, and what is the smallest first piece of it?

Take that smallest piece, and do it before today's walk is over: a message, a call, a decision to ask. If it is too big for the day, cut it in half. Then walk on and see how the rest of the day feels with the thing begun.

spans.t: At the end of the day

Do not decide anything tonight. That is the first piece of advice, and perhaps the most useful. A body that has walked a long way, and a mind that has taken in a long day, are bad judges of large things. Augustine's garden scene happens in the middle of a day, with a friend close by and a night's sleep still ahead. Anything of yours that needs deciding deserves the same: daylight, company and a night's sleep still to come.

So, only a look back. Did you take the small step? If you did, notice how it was. It may have been over very quickly, and felt out of proportion to the weeks of worry. That is a common way of such things. The step is often smaller than the wait.
If you did not, be gentle.
All but

is a respectable place to stand. Augustine stood there for a long time and wrote a book about it. Look at what held you back, as honestly as you can, and without any scolding. Was it fear? Tiredness? A reasonable doubt? Or just the long habit of the old way? Naming it is a step of its own.
Think also about the tomorrow of the passage. He tells us that he asked himself
How long, how long
, and then
tomorrow, and tomorrow
, and the question is also yours. There is a good tomorrow and a bad one. The good one is a real day, with a place in it for a small thing already chosen. The bad one is a name we give to never.

Then think of the voices that arrived unasked. A child calling across a yard, a bell, a stranger's passing remark that landed somewhere odd. None of them need be treated as a command. Augustine himself hesitates over the voice he heard. But a day with open ears gathers more than a day with closed ones, and it is a modest kind of attention to go back over what reached you without being asked.

And who sat beside you? On a road there is nearly always someone, a fellow walker, a person on the phone, a face on the next bunk. They may not know that they were doing anything. Tonight you might thank one of them, in a few words, for the silence they kept while you struggled.

If you took the small step and the day felt lighter after it, take note. Lightness is a kind of information. It does not prove that the step was right, but it tells you something about the weight of the delay, which was probably heavier than the deed.

A word about weeping. Augustine goes away to be alone for it, and Alypius, astonished, lets him go. If today brought tears, from a struggle or from nothing you can name, they belong in the day as much as the kilometres do.

items.t: What did I all but do today?
What would I do now if I were not waiting to feel ready?
Who sat beside me, in silence or in kindness, while something in me struggled?

spans.t: A short prayer

Tonight I stand where I stood this morning, close to the edge, breathing. I ask for no sudden light. Give me one small step, and the courage to take it, and a friend beside me while I do. Forgive me the days I only stood. Let me sleep, and wake to a real tomorrow.
What would you have to hush, in order to hear?
The passage

paras.t: The day now approaching whereon she was to depart this life (which day Thou well knewest, we knew not), it came to pass, Thyself, as I believe, by Thy secret ways so ordering it, that she and I stood alone, leaning in a certain window, which looked into the garden of the house where we now lay, at Ostia; where removed from the din of men, we were recruiting from the fatigues of a long journey, for the voyage. … And while we were discoursing and panting after her, we slightly touched on her with the whole effort of our heart; and we sighed, and there we leave bound the first fruits of the Spirit; and returned to vocal expressions of our mouth, where the word spoken has beginning and end. … "Lay," she saith, "this body any where; let not the care for that any way disquiet you: this only I request, that you would remember me at the Lord's altar, wherever you be." … "Nothing is far to God; nor was it to be feared lest at the end of the world, He should not recognise whence He were to raise me up."

spans.t: Reflection

There is a certain kind of evening, near the end of a long day, when you find a window. The room behind you is full of bags and boots and the noise of people sorting themselves out. In front of you there is a garden, or a yard, or a strip of darkening hill. Someone you care for is beside you. You say very little, and for a few minutes the day is exactly the right size.
That is where the ninth book of the
Confessions

brings us. Augustine and his mother are in a house at Ostia, the harbour town of Rome, on their way back to Africa. They have come a long way and are waiting for a ship. The passage begins with the sentence that sets the scene: they stood alone,
leaning in a certain window, which looked into the garden of the house
removed from the din of men
recruiting from the fatigues of a long journey
. That last phrase could be written on any pilgrim's wall. Before all of it, in a bracket, stands a quiet sadness: the day of her death was near,
which day Thou well knewest, we knew not
What they talk about is the largest subject there is. They ask what the eternal life of the saints might be like. Augustine then tries to say what they imagined. Suppose everything were hushed.
If to any the tumult of the flesh were hushed, hushed the images of earth, and waters, and air
, he writes,
hushed also the pole of heaven, yea the very soul be hushed to herself

. The sentence runs on and on. Suppose every sign and every voice went quiet, even the voice of creation, and then suppose the one who made it all spoke by himself, with no word of flesh or angel or thunder in between. He ends by asking,
were not this, Enter into thy Master's joy?

It is a very long sentence, and it is built on a single word, said again and again. It is easy to lose the thread, and the thread is this. Everything we hear is a message about something else. Augustine imagines what it would be if all of it fell quiet and the thing itself was there.
