After the book's long story of her tears and his evasions, it is a relief to see the two of them simply talking, side by side, about what they both want. He is in his thirty-third year, and she is in her fifty-sixth. For a few minutes they are not mother and wayward son. They are two people at a window.
Then the passage turns, honestly, to how little they got. They
slightly touched
it, he says,
with the whole effort of our heart
. They sighed. And they
returned to vocal expressions of our mouth, where the word spoken has beginning and end

. That is the line to remember. The moment was short. They did not live in it. They came back to speech, which starts and stops, and went on being people in a house at Ostia. This scene is often described as an ecstasy. Augustine's own account is more modest, and more useful.

Within about five days his mother fell ill with a fever. On the ninth day of her sickness she died, in the fifty-sixth year of her age and the thirty-third of his, as he tells us. The passage quotes the two things she said that matter to a walker. She asked that they lay her body anywhere, and
let not the care for that any way disquiet you
. She wanted only to be remembered, at the altar. And when friends asked whether she was not afraid to die so far from home:
Nothing is far to God.

Three things are hard here. The hush sentence is hard going, and we have given you only its first lines. Read it aloud, slowly, for its rhythm, and do not worry if you lose the argument. The request to be remembered
at the Lord's altar

belongs to the Catholic practice of praying for the dead, and some readers will hold it differently. And the story does not explain itself. The conversation at the window is followed within days by her death, and Augustine draws no moral from the order of events. He only tells it.

So what does the day need? First, a window in it. Not an hour. Ten quiet minutes, with the din a little way off. Second, one person given your whole attention, as he gave his mother his. Third, an acceptance that it will not last, and that coming back to ordinary speech is not a failure. It is how the day goes on.
For the walk

items.t: What would I have to hush, to hear what this day is saying?

For ten minutes, walk without talk, music or phone. If you are with others, ask them for the quiet out loud: "Shall we have ten minutes?" You may find that they are glad to be asked. When the ten minutes are over, notice the moment you go back to speaking.

spans.t: At the end of the day
Find a window, if you can, or a door that opens on something that is not a screen. A courtyard, a hill, a street with the light going. Stand there for as long as it takes to hear the day quieten.

You have done a great deal today without being asked to describe it. The kilometres, the food, the faces, the weather, the small decisions: all of it has been carried by a body that will want to sleep soon. For a few minutes, let it be the window and not the room. The passage does not ask you to think about eternity. It asks only that you stand where the noise is a little way off, and let the hush be as large as it chooses.

Think of the conversation of the day that mattered most. Not the loudest one. Was there one, with someone, in which you were not hurrying to be somewhere else? A few quiet sentences at a table, a long walk side by side that arrived somewhere. If there was, remember who said what, and be glad of it. If there was not, no one has failed. It may be waiting tomorrow, with the next stranger who sits down beside you.

A small practice, if the evening allows it: turn off one thing more than you usually would. A phone, a speaker, a second conversation. Make the room one sound quieter than it was, and sit in the difference for a minute. If you are not alone in the room, you can still make a window of a kind. The people around you are also finishing their day, and a quiet good night across the room is a small hush of its own.
And think of the people who are far away tonight. Augustine's mother was a long way from her own country, and her last thoughts were about distance.
Nothing is far to God
is her comfort, and a believer will hear it as a promise. If you do not believe, it can still be heard as a wish for anyone who is far from home tonight: that they are not as far away as they feel.
You may feel nothing special, and that is allowed. Augustine's conversation has been called a vision. Yours may be an ordinary evening. Both are good.

An honest word about tiredness. Quiet may come more easily when you are worn out, and it can be hard to tell the hush of rest from the hush of exhaustion. Either is welcome tonight. Neither needs a name. Do not try to make the evening into a vision.
If there is someone you want to be remembered by, or someone you want to remember tonight, say the name once, quietly, before you sleep. It is a small thing, and it is not nothing.

items.t: Whom did I talk with today, unhurried, about something that mattered?
What did I manage to hush, even for a minute?
Whom would I like to remember tonight, or be remembered by?

spans.t: A short prayer

Tonight I stand at the window of the day. Let the noise go a little way off. Keep those who are far from me, and let them know they are not forgotten. Thank you for the talk that mattered, and the quiet after it. Let me rest, and let the morning find me gentle.
Where did you walk today, and where were you?
The passage

paras.t: And I come to the fields and spacious palaces of my memory, where are the treasures of innumerable images, brought into it from things of all sorts perceived by the senses. … And men go abroad to admire the heights of mountains, the mighty billows of the sea, the broad tides of rivers, the compass of the ocean, and the circuits of the stars, and pass themselves by; nor wonder that when I spake of all these things, I did not see them with mine eyes, yet could not have spoken of them, unless I then actually saw the mountains, billows, rivers, stars which I had seen, and that ocean which I believe to be, inwardly in my memory, and that, with the same vast spaces between, as if I saw them abroad. … Too late loved I Thee, O Thou Beauty of ancient days, yet ever new! too late I loved Thee! And behold, Thou wert within, and I abroad, and there I searched for Thee; deformed I, plunging amid those fair forms which Thou hadst made. Thou wert with me, but I was not with Thee. Things held me far from Thee, which, unless they were in Thee, were not at all. Thou calledst, and shoutedst, and burstest my deafness. Thou flashedst, shonest, and scatteredst my blindness. Thou breathedst odours, and I drew in breath and panted for Thee. I tasted, and hunger and thirst. Thou touchedst me, and I burned for Thy peace.

spans.t: Reflection

Lie down at the end of a mountain day and close your eyes, and the hill is still there. The bend where the path doubled back. The colour of the rock at the pass. The cold of a stream on your wrists. None of it is in front of you, and all of it can be seen, with its distances intact. Where, exactly, is it?
The tenth book of the
Confessions

begins with that question. The first nine books were the story of a life, from the cradle to the death of his mother. Now the story stops, and Augustine says plainly what he will do instead. He will tell his reader, he writes,
not what I have been, but what I now am and what I yet am
. The rest of the book looks inward, and he starts with memory.

This is a hard stretch for a first-time reader. Books ten to thirteen are philosophy and scripture more than story, and a reader who loved the pear tree and the garden may feel the ground change underfoot. Memory is the easiest of the four to enter, and the passage gives only a taste of it.
He calls it a country.
I come to the fields and spacious palaces of my memory, where are the treasures of innumerable images
, he says,
brought into it from things of all sorts perceived by the senses.
He walks into it as you might walk into a house: fields, palaces, rooms behind rooms. In the pages that follow he wonders at it for a long time. In
darkness and silence
he can call up colours at will; he can recall a song with his mouth shut. Nobody put the images in a drawer. They are simply there, with the vast spaces between them, as if he saw them abroad.
Then comes a sentence that a mountain walker is likely to feel.
And men go abroad to admire the heights of mountains, the mighty billows of the sea, the broad tides of rivers, the compass of the ocean, and the circuits of the stars, and pass themselves by.

It stings, a little, as the first day's sentence about feet did. The sentence does not say that you should not admire a mountain. It says that people travel far to wonder at a mountain and never turn to wonder at the thing that holds it. Augustine finds the mountain he remembers, inside, with its distances intact. You are the place where the mountains are kept.
Next, the line for which the whole book is perhaps best known.
Too late loved I Thee, O Thou Beauty of ancient days, yet ever new!
It is a cry, and also a thanksgiving. He is late, and he has been found.
Thou wert within, and I abroad, and there I searched for Thee; deformed I, plunging amid those fair forms which Thou hadst made.
The thing he was looking for far off was nearer than the search. Then the rhythm quickens, and all five senses arrive in turn:
Thou calledst, and shoutedst
, for the ears,
Thou flashedst, shonest
, for the eyes,
Thou breathedst odours
, for the nose,
I tasted
, and
Thou touchedst me
. It is a reminder that he did not meet what he sought by thinking alone. You have used all five of yours today.

Three things need saying. The first is that it is a sharp thing to be told, in a book that goes with a road, that the road may be the wrong place to look. Take it as half a sentence. The other half is that the road may be the best place to begin looking in, since a long walk empties the head of its usual noise. The second is that
deformed

is harsh. Augustine's picture of himself plunging among the fair things of the world and not seeing their source can feel like a verdict on loving the world at all. Read the next lines as a correction: the beauty was a real beauty, only not the last one. The third is that it is addressed to God, and a reader who does not share that may hear
Thou wert within
as a puzzle. One way in is this: whatever you are looking for out there is perhaps nearer than the looking.
So what might it change in a day? A modest thing. To look at something long enough that it goes in. And, from time to time, to turn from the view to the one who is viewing.
For the walk

items.t: What am I passing by, in myself, while I look at the mountains?

Choose one thing on the road, a rock face, a gate, a bend of a stream, and look at it for a full minute, as if you will be asked tonight to describe it. Then walk on and see how much of it you can find this evening, with your eyes closed. You do not need to remember it perfectly. The point is to look at one thing properly.

spans.t: At the end of the day
Here is the evening's work, and it is lighter than it sounds. Lie down, if you can, and close your eyes. Then walk the day again, without moving.

Start with the first hour. A door, a step, the cold air. Let the images arrive in their order, and do not force them. Then the middle: a long slope, a bend, a village, a meal. Notice which pictures come up bright and which have already gone grey. The ones that come back brightly are the ones you were really looking at. The grey ones are the ones you passed by.

Augustine is amazed that the mind can do this, and tells us that in darkness and silence he can summon colour at will. You may find the same. If a place has stayed with you in such detail that you could walk it again, give it a moment's thanks. If very little has stayed, that is not a failure, and it is useful to know. Perhaps you were looking at your own feet, or at your own thoughts, and the mountains were only behind them.

Think of the five senses. Which of them had the best day? A road like this feeds them all. Cold water on the tongue, wood smoke or cut grass in the air, the sound of bells or a stream, the pull of the slope in your legs, the colour of the hills as the light moves. If one was missing today, because you were too tired or too hurried or too far inside your own head, you might give it a little more room tomorrow.

Then turn the same attention round, as the passage suggests, from the view to the one who views. Ask in plain words how you are. Not what you did, but how it is in there. Tired, certainly. Hungry, perhaps. Glad, or low, or somewhere between. Give each of those a single word and leave it at that. It is the nearest thing to an inward walk that a worn-out evening allows, and it takes less than a minute.
Too late

is not a sentence for tonight. You are not too late for anything this evening, except supper. Augustine wrote that cry as a man who had been found, and a cry of that kind looks back with relief and does not sulk. If you find something within yourself tonight that you wish you had noticed years ago, treat it as welcome.

Tiredness has a plain use here, and a kind one. A body that has finished its work leaves a good deal of room for memory, and sleep does a good deal of the filing of what you have gathered, whether or not you approve.
If you are too tired to walk the whole day again, walk half of it: only the morning, or only the last hour. A short memory kept is worth more than a long one lost.

items.t: What did I take in today that I would like to keep?
Where was I abroad today, in my head or my phone, while something waited within?
Which of my five senses had the best day, and which needs more room tomorrow?

spans.t: A short prayer

Tonight I close my eyes and walk the day again. Thank you for what I saw, and for what I only half saw. Let me not pass myself by. Whatever I am looking for, let it be nearer than my looking. Keep what I have gathered, and let me sleep.
How long is an hour on a road?
The passage

paras.t: For what is time? Who can readily and briefly explain this? Who can even in thought comprehend it, so as to utter a word about it? But what in discourse do we mention more familiarly and knowingly, than time? And, we understand, when we speak of it; we understand also, when we hear it spoken of by another. … What then is time? If no one asks me, I know: if I wish to explain it to one that asketh, I know not: yet I say boldly that I know, that if nothing passed away, time past were not; and if nothing were coming, a time to come were not; and if nothing were, time present were not. Those two times then, past and to come, how are they, seeing the past now is not, and that to come is not yet? But the present, should it always be present, and never pass into time past, verily it should not be time, but eternity. … Yea, that one hour passeth away in flying particles. Whatsoever of it hath flown away, is past; whatsoever remaineth, is to come.

spans.t: Reflection

There is an hour in most long days that will not pass. It is usually early in the afternoon, on a stretch that is straight and flat and exactly the colour of the one before it. You look at your watch. Eleven minutes have gone by. You walk on, and look again, and it is nine. Then, later, there is another hour, at a table or on a bench, with someone you like, and you look up and the light has changed and it is evening.
It is the same hour, in the same number of minutes. And yet it is not. The eleventh book of the
Confessions
is a long, patient attempt to say what is going on.
Augustine does not begin with a theory. He begins with a small, honest embarrassment:
What then is time? If no one asks me, I know: if I wish to explain it to one that asketh, I know not.

It is a very good sentence. We all use the word every minute of the day, and all of us understand each other. The moment someone asks us to say what it is, it slips out of our hands. You know a good many things in that way: what home is, what a good day is, what you mean when you say you are tired.
Then he tries. The past is gone, so it is not. The future has not come, so it is not yet. So only the present is left. But
the present, should it always be present, and never pass into time past, verily it should not be time, but eternity.
The present only counts as time because it is on its way out. That is a curious thing to say about the one moment you are sure of.

The third stretch of the passage drives it home. Take a century, he says a little further on, and only one year of it can be present. Take that year, and only one month. Take the month, and one day. Take the day, and one hour. At last he arrives at the hour you are in, and it will not stay still either:
that one hour passeth away in flying particles.
Whatsoever of it hath flown away, is past; whatsoever remaineth, is to come.
If you try to hold the present, there is nothing to hold. A few lines later he says it outright, in a short sentence worth keeping:
The present hath no space.

Where does that leave a walker, with eleven minutes on the watch and the afternoon dragging? Not with a plain answer, and Augustine is honest about that. Later in the book he proposes, tentatively, that time is held in the mind. There is a
present of things past
, which is memory; a
present of things present
, which is sight; and a
present of things future

, which is expectation. On that picture, one might say that the long afternoon is long because your expectation is stretched towards the end of it, and the pleasant evening is short because you were wholly in the sight of it. That is a walker's gloss, not his, and it is not a proof. He keeps saying as much himself as he goes:
I ask, Father, I affirm not
. He is thinking aloud, and asking for help.

It is worth noticing that the book in your hand is itself an example. Nine books of memory, and then a prayer that leans forward into what is not yet known: Augustine's own mind, stretched across time as he writes. He does not say so here. The passage is only the place where he stops, in the middle of a prayer, to ask how such a thing is possible at all.

Two difficulties, then. This is a place where a reader may lose patience. It is a puzzle about words, and a reader may well wonder what it has to do with a Camino. Fair. You can hold it lightly. The second is that it will not shorten a single afternoon. A philosopher's argument does not lengthen the daylight.

What it can do is smaller, and it is not Augustine's claim but a use that a walker might make of it. If the present is never all there at once, and only the moment you are in is real, then an unbearable hour is not an hour at all. It is only this step, and this breath, followed by another. The hill is long. The step is short. You may find that this is a comfort at four in the afternoon, and you may find that it is not. It costs nothing to try.
For the walk

items.t: How long is this hour? Not by the watch, but as it feels.

For the next hour, do not look at a watch or a phone. Guess when it is over, then check. Notice what the guess says about how you spent it. Do not mind if you cheat and look. The point is the guessing. If the hour was long, ask what you were stretching towards. If it was short, ask what held you.

spans.t: At the end of the day

Some days are measured in kilometres and some in hours, and tonight you can look at the day by neither. Think of it as a day made of stretches that were different from one another in length, whatever the clock said.

Which hours vanished? There was probably one. A good conversation, a pleasant meal, an hour on a bench in the sun. You looked up and it was gone. On his picture, you were wholly in the sight of them. Those hours are worth naming, because you may want to find your way back to them tomorrow.

Which dragged? Perhaps the long flat stretch, perhaps an afternoon of wanting to arrive. Be fair to it. A dragging hour is often an hour in which part of you was somewhere else: in the next village, the next meal, the end of the day. There is nothing wrong with the wish to arrive. But a good deal of the road passes through the hours you were waiting to get through.

What were you waiting for? Not a grand thing, perhaps. A rest, a shower, a message. If the waiting took more of the day than the thing itself, that is an ordinary human result, and worth a smile. Most of life is spent between one thing and another.

A road gives days clear edges: wake, walk, stop, eat, sleep. It is an unusual gift to have hours with so little else to do but be the hours they are, and tonight you can see the shape of the day as you rarely can at home. Give it three words, one for the fast hour, one for the slow hour and one for an hour in between. It is a very small diary, and it will be enough to bring the day back in a year.

Then try the oddest part of Augustine's argument, just once, as an experiment, before you sleep. Take a single breath, and notice that this breath is the whole of what is happening. Not the day behind, which is memory, and not the day to come, which is expectation. Only the breath you are in. It will be over before you finish noticing, which is about as close as a breath can come to his argument.

Tonight's tiredness is a very physical kind of time. Your body has measured the day in its own way, in muscles and soles and shoulders, and its measure is usually truer than the watch's. Let it be the clock tonight. When it says that it is time to sleep, it is probably right. It has been keeping time all day without being asked, and it has not been wrong yet.

items.t: Which hour of today do I want to keep, and which am I glad to let pass?
What was I waiting for today, and did the waiting take more of the day than the thing itself?
What am I actually doing in this breath, and is that enough?

spans.t: A short prayer

Tonight I thank you for the hours that flew and the hours that dragged. Forgive me the time I wished away. Let me be where I am, as far as I am able. Keep what has passed, and hold what has not yet come. Let my body keep its own good time, and let me sleep.

chapters.title: Day 12. Where do we see it?

spans.t: How do we read together what none of us can finish reading?
The passage

paras.t: My heart, O Lord, touched with the words of Thy Holy Scripture, is much busied, amid this poverty of my life. And therefore most times, is the poverty of human understanding copious in words, because enquiring hath more to say than discovering, and demanding is longer than obtaining, and our hand that knocks, hath more work to do, than our hand that receives. … The lowliness of my tongue confesseth unto Thy Highness, that Thou madest heaven and earth; this heaven which I see, and this earth that I tread upon, whence is this earth that I bear about me; Thou madest it. … For this brotherly and peaceful word do I return unto Him: "If we both see that to be true that Thou sayest, and both see that to be true that I say, where, I pray Thee, do we see it? Neither I in thee, nor thou in me; but both in the unchangeable Truth itself, which is above our souls." … So when one says, "Moses meant as I do"; and another, "Nay, but as I do," I suppose that I speak more reverently, "Why not rather as both, if both be true?"

spans.t: Reflection

Two people at a table are looking at the same map and disagree. The road offers a choice at one point, a higher way or a lower one, and each of them is quite sure which is right. One has read something. The other has heard something from a friend. They are polite about it for a while. Then one of them says that the other is simply wrong, and the evening goes a little cold.

For that choice, a book of readings is not the place to look. Weather and conditions change, and the answer belongs to current information and local advice. But the table is a good place to read the twelfth book of the
Confessions
, because it is about what to do when people read the same words and see different things.
Here is the plain situation. Book twelve is probably the hardest of the thirteen. Augustine takes the first line of Genesis, the story of creation in the Bible, and tries to say what
heaven and earth
means in it, and what the
earth invisible and without form
was, and what became of what he calls the
heaven of heavens
. It is the kind of thing a first-time reader nods at for a page and then loses. Augustine knows it. He even asks, at one point,
what reader would hold out to take in the whole?
We have not tried to carry you through it. We have taken the three places where it steps back and says something a walker can hold.
The first is the opening.
My heart, O Lord, touched with the words of Thy Holy Scripture, is much busied
, he says, and then:
enquiring hath more to say than discovering, and demanding is longer than obtaining, and our hand that knocks, hath more work to do, than our hand that receives.

It is a very plain description of seeking. The asking takes longer than the finding, and the hand that knocks is busier than the hand that is handed something. Anyone who has asked for directions and been given a long answer will know it.
The second is a short sentence about the ground. The creation he is trying to understand is not far away. He says:
this heaven which I see, and this earth that I tread upon, whence is this earth that I bear about me; Thou madest it.
The earth he is walking on is the earth he is asking about. For a walker that is a nice small turn: the thing under your boots is the thing he is asking about.
The third is the heart of the passage. People differ about what Moses meant. One says one thing and another says another, and each is sure. Augustine imagines saying to one of them:

If we both see that to be true that Thou sayest, and both see that to be true that I say, where, I pray Thee, do we see it? Neither I in thee, nor thou in me; but both in the unchangeable Truth itself, which is above our souls.
The point is delicate. If we both see a thing is true, we are not seeing it in each other. We are both looking at the same thing, and it belongs to neither of us. Then, in the last lines:
Why not rather as both, if both be true?
A few lines before this passage, in words we have left out, he says it more broadly:
Thy truth is neither mine, nor his, nor another's.
Truth, in his picture, is public, like the road. Elsewhere in the book he compares a short sacred text to a spring: a small source that feeds more streams than any one of the streams could.
Two cautions. First,
both
is not a blanket. Augustine is clear that some claims are simply false, and he has no patience with people who think they know them to be true:
away with all those who imagine themselves to know as a truth, what is false.

The generosity applies when two readings are both true. It does not say that every opinion is as good as every other. Second, the whole conversation is about the Bible, and it takes the authority of that book for granted. A reader who does not share it can still hear the manner: how to disagree without making it a fight over who owns the light.
So how would this look at the next table? Slow down before you say that someone is wrong. Ask what they can see from where they sit. And ask yourself the question that is the day's title.
For the walk

items.t: What am I sure of that someone near me sees differently?

In your next conversation where you differ, ask the other person to say what they see, and say it back to them before you answer. If you are alone, do it in your head with a person you recently argued with, and see what is left of the argument. If there is no disagreement today, choose a small difference of taste with someone and ask about it with real curiosity.

spans.t: At the end of the day

Arguments on the road are usually small, and very few of them are about anything. Which way, how early, whose turn. They are worth looking at all the same, because they are made of the same stuff as the large ones.

Look back for a disagreement you had today, or one you only had in your head. It might have been over a route, or a bunk, or a remark in the kitchen. Where did it stand at the end? Resolved, shelved, still warm? Whichever it was, ask Augustine's question. Where, exactly, were the two of you looking? Sometimes the honest answer is that you were looking at different things, and had not noticed.

Now find the true thing in the other person's view. It is nearly always there, and nearly always smaller than they think and larger than you thought. It might be as little as the fact that they were tired. It might be a good point about the weather. If you can find it tonight, you can be gentler with the person tomorrow, which is more than a victory would have given you.

The other half of the passage is easier to miss. Augustine is willing, in this very book, to confess that he does not know what Moses meant. Was there a place today where you could have said as much, and did not? A route, a fact, a rumour you repeated with more confidence than you had? It costs something to admit it. It also saves a good deal. A day in which you owned up once, and meant it, to not knowing is a day on a stable footing.

Try one more thing before you sleep. Name something that you and the person you disagreed with both see clearly: a hill, a hot afternoon, an empty stomach. Begin from the light you share. And if there is a step, a wall or a patch of ground within reach, lay the flat of your hand on it for a breath. It is the earth that Augustine was asking about, and it has carried you all day.
You do not need to settle any of this tonight. The earth you tread on will be there in the morning, and so, probably, will the table.

Tiredness can make people quick to take offence. If you are feeling sharp at the edges tonight, it may not be anyone's fault, and it may be best to leave all the arguments of the day exactly where they are until you have slept. They will not spoil. Most of them will be smaller in the morning, and some will have gone altogether.

A last small thing. If the disagreement was with someone who is still beside you tonight, a plain, neutral sentence will do: "I was thinking about what you said." It claims nothing, and it costs very little.

items.t: Where did I insist on being right today?
What was true in a view I did not share?
Where could I have said that I did not know, and what would it have cost me?

spans.t: A short prayer

Tonight I lay down my arguments, the won ones and the lost ones. Thank you for the people who see differently from me. Let me look for the light we share, and not for the corner where I am right. Teach me to say that I do not know. Let me rest, and let the truth be larger than my opinion.

chapters.title: Day 13. Our rest is our place

spans.t: What carries you, and where does it set you down?
The passage

paras.t: In Thy Gift we rest; there we enjoy Thee. Our rest is our place. Love lifts us up thither, and Thy good Spirit lifts up our lowliness from the gates of death. In Thy good pleasure is our peace. The body by its own weight strives towards its own place. Weight makes not downward only, but to his own place. Fire tends upward, a stone downward. They are urged by their own weight, they seek their own places. … When out of their order, they are restless; restored to order, they are at rest. My weight, is my love; thereby am I borne, whithersoever I am borne. We are inflamed, by Thy Gift we are kindled; and are carried upwards; we glow inwardly, and go forwards. … O Lord God, give peace unto us: (for Thou hast given us all things;) the peace of rest, the peace of the Sabbath, which hath no evening. … Let it be asked of Thee, sought in Thee, knocked for at Thee; so, so shall it be received, so shall it be found, so shall it be opened. Amen.

spans.t: Reflection

At the end of a walking day, you take off the pack. Do it slowly, once, and notice what happens. For a moment your shoulders do not know what to do with themselves. Your whole body leans a little towards the nearest bench, like a stone towards the ground. A weight that you had stopped feeling has gone, and what was under it, tiredness, comes up to say hello. Then you sit, and the body settles as though it had been looking for that exact spot all day.
The last book of the
Confessions
has a picture for this. Augustine is thinking about why anything goes anywhere, and he answers with weight.
The body by its own weight strives towards its own place.
Fire tends upward, a stone downward. Each thing is urged by its weight to seek its place.
When out of their order, they are restless; restored to order, they are at rest.
That is a word you have met before. On the first day of this book, he said
our heart is restless, until it repose in Thee
, and here, on the last day, the same thought comes round again. Restlessness is a thing out of its place. Rest is arrival.
Our rest is our place
, he says, which is a short and rather beautiful sentence. Where you rest is where you belong.

Notice what the sentence does not say. It does not make rest the opposite of the road. It makes rest the place the road arrives at, the thing you were being carried towards all along. On that picture a pilgrimage is not a flight from rest. It is the long way round to it.
Then the line that matters most:
My weight, is my love; thereby am I borne, whithersoever I am borne.
On Day 7 the word to keep was
weight

, because it pulled Augustine down. Here it has turned. It may be that the weight that drags and the weight that carries are one thing seen from two ends. What you love is what carries you. It gets you up in the morning and takes you over the hill, and it is also the thing that will carry you to the place where you put the pack down. He says that
we glow inwardly, and go forwards
, which is as good a description of a walker as any in the book.

The passage then jumps to the end of the whole work. Book thirteen, the one we are in, reads the days of creation in Genesis as a long picture of the Church and the soul, and it is hard going. We have left all that. We join it as it finishes, with a prayer:
give peace unto us
the peace of rest, the peace of the Sabbath, which hath no evening.

Of the seven days of Genesis, the first six end with evening and morning. The seventh does not. Augustine makes much of that, and reads it as a day that does not close. A day that does not have to end because the work is done.
And the last sentence of the book is not a conclusion. It is a request.
Let it be asked of Thee, sought in Thee, knocked for at Thee; so, so shall it be received, so shall it be found, so shall it be opened. Amen.
Thirteen books of questions, and the last instruction is to go on asking.

A few things are hard here. The first is the physics. Fire going up and stones going down because of their natural places is ancient science, and it is no longer how we explain falling. Keep the picture and let the science go. Water finds its level, and so, he is saying, does a heart. The second is that
My weight, is my love

does not tell you whether the thing you love is good for you. It says only that love carries you somewhere. The question of what to love is left to you, and it is the real question. The third is the Sabbath. Augustine means the rest of eternal life, after all our works. For a tired person in a bunk, that may feel a long way off. The passage gives a taste before then, in the lines about the gift in which we rest and the peace that goes with it. It does not promise that you will feel it tonight.

So how might this go into a day? Loosely. By noticing what you love enough to carry, and by letting yourself rest when you arrive. A walker who cannot rest has not finished walking. And by ending, as the book does, with a question left open.
For the walk

items.t: What carries me? What do I love, that gets me over the next hill?

At your next stop, take the pack off slowly and sit. Before you reach for a drink, a phone or a map, let your body find its rest for one full minute. Notice where it settles. That settling is Augustine's picture, in a small way, at work in you.

spans.t: At the end of the day
This is the last evening of the book, and it may or may not be the evening of the end of your road. Either way, it is a good one for resting.

The body knows how. A day on foot has done its weighing, and it will tell you the answer in the usual way: heavy legs, loose shoulders, a slow wish for horizontal. Tonight there is nothing to improve. Augustine's Sabbath is a day without an evening, but yours has one, and it is a good one. Let it be the kind of evening that does not ask you to finish anything.

Look back, quite gently, at what carried you. A person, a hope, a stubbornness, a hunger for the next village. It does not have to be grand. For some of us it is a plain wish to see the next view, or to finish what we started. If you were carried today by something you love, name it. If you were carried only by habit, or by the group, or by fear of stopping, name that too, without fuss. It is useful to know which weight is doing the work.

Then think of the nearest thing to rest you found today. It might have been a bench, or a long drink, or a few minutes when nobody wanted anything of you. It might have been the moment you took the pack off, as in the morning's reading. If you cannot think of one, make it now: sit up, put your feet flat, and let the weight of your body go into the bed.

If you want one more look, take it at the whole of the book and not only the day. Thirteen readings, thirteen evenings. Is there one that stays with you, a sentence, a scene, a question? You need not know why. Augustine is not a comfortable companion, but he is an honest one, and the day that stays is usually the one that was honest with you.

The book you have been reading for thirteen days began with a heart that could not rest and ends with a request to be given rest. It does not claim that the request has been granted. It ends in the act of asking, and tonight that is enough. You can go to sleep in the middle of a question and trust the morning to hold it.

Tiredness has come all the way with you, from the first day. It is not an enemy of the pilgrimage. It is, more often than not, the shape that the day takes when you have spent yourself on something. Honour it. If you are too tired to ask for anything, the sentence for tonight is only: thank you, and good night.

items.t: What carried me today, and what did I love enough to keep walking for?
Where did I find the nearest thing to rest?
What am I asking for, as I go to sleep?

spans.t: A short prayer

Tonight I ask for rest. I ask in the middle of the day's dust, with my boots by the bed. Let what I love carry me, and let it be worth carrying. Where I have not found my place, let me stop pretending I have. Thank you for the road. Let me sleep like one who is home.

You have come to the end of the thirteen days, or you have stopped early, or you are reading them again. All three are fine. This book has no certificate to give you. It was made to keep a little company on a hard road, and a road has no use for a book once it is over, except to be remembered kindly.
So the only question left is what to keep. Not everything. Three small things will do.

items.t: A word.
Restless
opened the book and
rest
closed it, with
weight
in between. Take whichever word did the most work for you, and say it on a day when you need it.
A window.
The ten quiet minutes of Day 9: no talk, no music, no phone, only the day going quiet. All it needs is a wall or a doorway to stand at.
A question.
Some of the evening questions will have gone on turning in your mind. Keep the one that did, and do not hurry to answer it. The
Confessions
itself ends by asking.

spans.t: If you keep all three for a month, you will have kept a good deal from a long book.
How to go on
Come back whenever you like. The days are short, and a day that said little the first time may say more the fifth. You can also go to the day that fits the week you are having.

items.t: If someone you love is out of reach, Day 3.
If you are carrying a loss, Day 4.
If there is something you keep putting off, Day 8.
If an argument has gone cold, Day 12.
If you cannot rest, Day 13.

spans.t: You might also read Augustine himself. The work is in the public domain, in the same translation, at Project Gutenberg, ebook number 3296. It runs to about 110,000 words, something like eight hours of quiet reading. The first nine books tell the story and are the easiest. The last four are the hardest. Some of it is strange, and some of it will not suit you. That is allowed. A book of this kind is not a test, and a passage that asks for more than you can give, or less than you hoped, can be left where it is.
A last word

Augustine began by saying that the heart is restless, and he finished by asking. He did not claim to have arrived. The last book is full of questions about creation and time and the meaning of a few lines of scripture, and its last sentence hands the matter to the reader: ask, seek, knock. It is an odd way to close a long book, and a good one. Nothing in it pretends that the restlessness was cured by thirteen days, or by a road.

You may or may not have reached Santiago. Either way, the road goes on from where you are. The thing you carried to the start came with you to the end, and it will come home with you, a little better known than before. That is not nothing. A heart that has been listened to is easier to live with.
Walk again when you can, even if it is only round the block with the phone left behind. And when the restlessness comes back, as it will, remember that Augustine thought it was the compass.
Buen Camino.
